**June 23, 1956 — Saturday**

This date was run once already in this session. What follows draws on different selections than the first.

---

**The Day Itself: Cairo's New President**

On the exact day of your birth, Egypt voted. Gamal Abdel Nasser — 38 years old, electric, and furious at a colonial order he had spent his adult life plotting to dismantle — was confirmed as president in a national referendum, the new constitution ratified alongside him. The margins were enormous. He had been Egypt's real power since the 1952 coup; now the formal architecture matched the fact. Thirty-three days later he would nationalize the Suez Canal, triggering a war that autumn involving Britain, France, and Israel, ending in American pressure forcing all three to stand down, and closing forever the era in which London and Paris could act as imperial powers without Washington's blessing. Your birth fell on the last day before Nasser lit that particular fuse.

**The Last Children of Polio**

Fourteen months before your birth, on April 12, 1955, Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective. The announcement had produced scenes of public jubilation unusual for a medical press conference — church bells, spontaneous celebrations, parents weeping with relief. By June 1956, mass vaccination programs were rolling out across the United States, and the long terror of polio summers — the seasonal dread that had kept children out of swimming pools, that had put iron lungs in hospital wards, that had paralyzed Franklin Roosevelt — was beginning to lift. You were born into the first cohort of American children who would grow up largely protected. The generation just before yours had lived with that fear as a normal condition of childhood. Yours mostly would not. That shift, invisible at the time, was one of the great gifts the year of your birth handed you.

**A Princess, Two Months Earlier**

On April 19, 1956 — sixty-five days before your birth — Grace Kelly, one of the most famous actresses in Hollywood, married Prince Rainier III of Monaco in a ceremony broadcast to millions across Europe and America. The wedding had consumed the international press for months. Kelly had won an Academy Award two years earlier and was filming *High Society* when she left Hollywood for Monaco permanently. The cultural appetite for that story — the American movie star becoming an actual princess — was essentially infinite. By the time you were born, the honeymoon photographs were still circulating. It was the kind of event that marked time: people remembered where they were when they heard, the way they would remember later events of a wholly different kind.

**Four Months from the Twin Disasters**

You were born four months before one of the strangest weeks of the Cold War. In late October and early November 1956, two crises erupted simultaneously, pulling the world's attention in opposite directions. In Hungary, a popular uprising against Soviet rule was crushed by tanks — thousands killed, two hundred thousand fleeing as refugees — while the world watched and the West did nothing beyond expressing horror. At the same time, Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt over Suez, were condemned by both the United States and the Soviet Union, and were forced into a humiliating withdrawal. Two empires collapsed in a single week: the Soviet empire's pretension to popularity, and the British and French empires' pretension to independent great-power action. You spent your first autumn on earth while all of that was happening.

**Television Taking Over**

The summer of your birth was the last presidential campaign season in which television was still finding its footing as the dominant medium. By 1956, more than three-quarters of American homes had a television set. The 1956 Republican and Democratic conventions were broadcast live, gavel to gavel. Eisenhower and Stevenson both bought television advertising. The medium had arrived completely — and with it came a new kind of political visibility, a new relationship between the public and its leaders' faces and voices, a new standard for what a candidate had to be. You grew up in the first generation for whom television was simply the air of the culture.

**Khrushchev's Gift to the Future**

Four months before your birth, Nikita Khrushchev had stood before the 20th Congress of the Communist Party and denounced Stalin — his purges, his paranoia, the millions he had killed. The speech was supposed to be secret. It leaked within weeks. For anyone paying attention, it meant the communist monolith had begun to crack from inside: its own leadership had admitted the crimes it had spent decades denying. The Hungarian uprising six months later was, in part, a consequence of that speech — of the hope it kindled that things could change. You were born into the first year in which the Soviet system's defenders had conceded, in secret and then not so secretly, that the Soviet system had done monstrous things.

**Seventy Years**

You are 70 years old. You were born the day Nasser became president, four months before Suez and Hungary remade the geopolitical map, into a world where polio had just been conquered and television had just taken over. The Cold War defined your childhood and then ended, abruptly and without a final battle, when you were 33. You watched the entire arc of the space age — from Sputnik, when you were one, through the moon landing at 13, through the shuttle era, and now into private rockets and planetary rovers. You have watched the world's dominant communications technology change completely three times in your adult life: from broadcast television to the personal computer to the internet to the smartphone.

---

The world you entered on that Saturday in June had just confirmed a president who would trigger a regional war in a month, was four months from one of its strangest geopolitical weeks, and was handing the first generation of vaccinated children a future without one of its oldest seasonal terrors. It was a world on the edge of several things at once — as most worlds are, though it is rarely so visible from the outside as it was in the summer of 1956.
